'''Richard Neil Zare''' (born November 19, 1939, in [[Cleveland]], Ohio) is the Marguerite Blake Wilbur Professor in Natural Science and a Professor of [[Chemistry]] at [[Stanford University]].<ref name="Presidential">{{cite web|title=Richard Zare – Marguerite Blake Wilbur Professor in Natural Science; Professor of Chemistry|url=http://paesmem.net/node/1566|website=Presidential Awards for Excellence in Science, Mathematics & Engineering Mentoring|access-date=March 28, 2017}}</ref> Throughout his career, Zare has made a considerable impact in [[physical chemistry]] and [[analytical chemistry]], particularly  through the development of [[laser-induced fluorescence]] (LIF) and the study of [[chemical reaction]]s at the molecular and nanoscale level.<ref name="Mukhopadhyay"/> LIF is an extremely sensitive technique with applications ranging from analytical chemistry and molecular biology to astrophysics.<ref name="KFIP"/> One of its applications was the sequencing of the [[human genome]].<ref name="Arnaud"/>

Zare is known for his enthusiasm for science and his exploration of new areas of research.<ref name="Bubbling"/>  He has mentored over 150 PhD students and postdoctoral researchers, of whom more than 49 are women or members of minorities.<ref name="Presidential"/> Zare is a strong advocate for women in science,<ref name="IX">{{cite journal|last1=Zare|first1=Richard N.|title=Sex, Lies, and Title IX Federal law banning sex discrimination in schools may do as much for academics as it has for athletics|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=May 15, 2006|volume=84|issue=20|pages=46–49|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/84/i20/Sex-Lies-Title-IX.html|access-date=March 28, 2017|doi=10.1021/cen-v084n020.p046|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and a fellow of the [[Association for Women in Science]] (AWIS) as of 2008.<ref name="Bubbling"/>

==Education==
Zare earned his BA in chemistry and physics in 1961 and his PhD in 1964 in physical and analytical chemistry at [[Harvard University]]. As an undergraduate he worked with [[William Klemperer]].<ref name="Bubbling"/> Zare moved to the [[University of California, Berkeley]] to do PhD work with [[Dudley Herschbach]], then returned 2 years later when Herschbach accepted a position at Harvard. Zare completed his PhD thesis, a theoretical analysis of ''Molecular fluorescence and photodissociation'',<ref>{{cite web|title=Molecular fluorescence and photodissociation. Zare, Richard Neil.|url=http://id.lib.harvard.edu/aleph/004034061/catalog|website=Harvard Library|access-date=March 28, 2017}}</ref> with Herschbach at Harvard in 1964.<ref name="Bubbling">{{cite journal|last1=Arnaud|first1=Celia Henry|title=Bubbling With Enthusiasm|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=March 22, 2010|volume=88|issue=12|pages=14–18|url=https://pubs.acs.org/cen/coverstory/88/8812cover.html|access-date=March 28, 2017|doi=10.1021/cen-v088n012.p014|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Career==
Zare joined [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] as an assistant professor in 1965. From 1966 to 1969, he was jointly appointed in the departments of chemistry, physics and astrophysics at [[JILA]] at the [[University of Colorado Boulder]].  In 1969 he became a full professor in the department of chemistry at [[Columbia University]].<ref name="Zarelab">{{cite web|title=About Richard N. Zare: Biosketch|url=https://web.stanford.edu/group/Zarelab/about.html|website=Zarelab|access-date=March 28, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Richard N. Zare, Stanford University|journal=The Analyst|date=2005|volume=130|issue=6|pages=798–9|doi=10.1039/B504927J|pmid=15915266|bibcode=2005Ana...130..798.}}</ref> He was named the Higgins Professor of Natural Science at Columbia in 1975.<ref name="KFIP">{{cite web|title=Professor Richard Zare Winner of the 2011 KFIP Prize for Science|url=http://kfip.org/professor-richard-zare/|website=King Faisal International Prize|access-date=March 29, 2017}}</ref>

In 1977 Zare accepted a position as a full professor of chemistry at [[Stanford University]], becoming the Marguerite Blake Wilbur Professor in Natural Science in 1987.  He served as chair of the chemistry department from 2005 to 2011.<ref name="Stanford">{{cite web|title=Dick Zare|url=https://chemistry.stanford.edu/people/dick-zare|website=Stanford University|access-date=March 28, 2017|archive-date=March 11, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170311060143/https://chemistry.stanford.edu/people/dick-zare|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Zare  served on the [[National Science Board]] (NSB) of the [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF) from 1990 to 1996, and was the board's chair from 1994 to 1996.<ref name="Bubbling"/>
He was a founding co-editor of the ''[[Annual Review of Analytical Chemistry]]'' from 2008–2012.<ref name="Zare">{{cite journal |last1=Yeung |first1=Edward S. |last2=Zare |first2=Richard N. |title=Preface |journal=Annual Review of Analytical Chemistry |date=June 13, 2008 |volume=1 |issue=1 |doi=10.1146/annurev.ac.061308.100001 |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.ac.061308.100001 |access-date=September 8, 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Co-editors of the Annual Review of Analytical Chemistry - Volume 5, 2012 |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/db/directory?2012,anchem |website=Annual Reviews Directory |access-date=September 8, 2021}}</ref>
He is a member of the editorial advisory boards of other scientific publications, among them ''[[Royal Society of Chemistry#Publications|Chemistry World]]'', ''[[Angewandte Chemie]]'', ''[[Central European Journal of Chemistry]]'', ''Journal of Separation Sciences'' and the ''Chinese Journal of Chromatography''.<ref name="Analyst">{{cite journal|title=Richard N. Zare, Stanford University|journal=The Analyst|date=2005|volume=130|issue=6|pages=798–799|doi=10.1039/b504927j|pmid=15915266|url=http://www.rsc.org/delivery/_ArticleLinking/DisplayHTMLArticleforfree.cfm?JournalCode=AN&Year=2005&ManuscriptID=b504927j&Iss=6|access-date=March 28, 2017|bibcode=2005Ana...130..798.|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
<ref name="Mukhopadhyay">{{cite journal|last1=Mukhopadhyay|first1=Rajendrani|title=A quest for fun|journal=Analytical Chemistry|date=November 2007|volume=79|issue=21|pages=7945–7947|doi=10.1021/ac071983m|pmid=18044020|url=https://web.stanford.edu/group/Zarelab/zare/071101_InMyShoes.pdf|access-date=March 28, 2017|doi-access=free}}</ref> 
Zare served on the Physical Sciences jury for the [[Infosys Prize]] from 2014 to 2016. 
He is chairman of the board of directors at [[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Reviews, Inc.]], and serves on the board of directors of [[The Camille and Henry Dreyfus Foundation]].<ref name="KFIP"/>

==Research==
[[File:Richard Zare - National Medal of Science, 1983.webm|thumb|Zare discusses his contributions to chemistry and molecular spectroscopy.]]
Zare is well known for his research in [[laser]] chemistry, particularly the development of laser-induced fluorescence, which he has used to study [[reaction dynamics]] and analytical detection methods.<ref name="Bubbling"/>  His research on the spectroscopy of chemical compounds suggested a new mechanism for energy transference in [[inelastic collisions]].<ref name="Bergeron">{{cite news|last1=Bergeron|first1=Louis|title=Results of research on atomic collisions fly in the face of conventional wisdom|url=http://news.stanford.edu/news/2008/july9/vibrate-070908.html|access-date=March 29, 2017|work=Stanford News|date=July 3, 2008}}</ref><ref name="tug">{{cite web|title=Radicals shake up molecules in a tug o' war|website=(e) Science News|date=July 3, 2008|url=http://esciencenews.com/articles/2008/07/03/radicals.shake.molecules.a.tug.o.war}}</ref><ref name="Greaves">{{cite journal|last1=Greaves|first1=Stuart J.|last2=Wrede|first2=Eckart|last3=Goldberg|first3=Noah T.|last4=Zhang|first4=Jianyang|last5=Miller|first5=Daniel J.|last6=Zare|first6=Richard N.|title=Vibrational excitation through tug-of-war inelastic collisions|journal=Nature|date=July 3, 2008|volume=454|issue=7200|pages=88–91|doi=10.1038/nature07079|pmid=18596807|bibcode=2008Natur.454...88G|s2cid=205213863}}</ref>
He and his students have developed tools and  techniques to examine [[chemical reaction]]s at the molecular and nanoscale levels. They have explored a wide-ranging variety of problems in physical chemistry and chemical analysis including examination of heterogeneous structures in mineral samples, the contents of cells and subcellular compartments, and the chemical analysis of liquid samples.<ref name="Stanford"/>

Early in his career, the question of whether laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) could be used to study [[aflatoxins]] spurred Zare to adapt LIF for use on liquids.  Work with postdoc Gerald Diebold resulted in the first use of LIF for detection in chemical analysis.<ref name="Bubbling"/><ref name="Hieftje">{{cite book|last1=Hieftje|first1=Gary M.|last2=Travis|first2=John C.|last3=Lytle|first3=Fred E.|title=Lasers in Chemical Analysis|date=1981|publisher=Humana Press|location=Totowa, NJ|isbn=978-1-4612-6009-7|pages=277|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DZe1BwAAQBAJ&pg=PA277}}</ref><ref name="Diebold">{{cite journal|last1=Diebold|first1=G.|last2=Zare|first2=R.|title=Laser fluorimetry: subpicogram detection of aflatoxins using high-pressure liquid chromatography|journal=Science|date=June 24, 1977|volume=196|issue=4297|pages=1439–1441|doi=10.1126/science.867038|pmid=867038|bibcode=1977Sci...196.1439D|s2cid=33734681}}</ref> 
This opened up the potential for a wide variety of fluid applications,<ref name="Bubbling"/> including the detection of single molecules in liquids at room-temperature<ref name="Nie">{{cite journal|last1=Nie|first1=S|last2=Chiu|first2=DT|last3=Zare|first3=RN|title=Probing individual molecules with confocal fluorescence microscopy.|journal=Science|date=November 11, 1994|volume=266|issue=5187|pages=1018–21|pmid=7973650|doi=10.1126/science.7973650|bibcode=1994Sci...266.1018N}}</ref> and detection methods for [[capillary electrophoresis]].<ref name="Cazes">{{cite book|last1=Cazes|first1=Jack|title=Encyclopedia of chromatography|date=2005|publisher=Taylor & Francis|location=Boca Raton, Florida|isbn=978-0-8247-2787-1|page=519|edition=2nd|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dOvTx01elfsC&pg=PA519|access-date=March 28, 2017}}</ref>
Zare and his coworkers have combined [[CCD imaging]] with LIF detection to detect amol and zeptamole amounts of FITC-labelled [[amino acids]].<ref name="Landers">{{cite book|last1=Landers|first1=James P.|title=Handbook of capillary electrophoresis|date=1997|publisher=CRC Press|location=Boca Raton|isbn=978-0-8493-2498-7|page=401|edition=2nd|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wn_dpL5OcKwC&pg=PA401}}</ref>
Zare and his students have also developed [[cavity ring-down spectroscopy]] (CRDS) for quantitative diagnosis,<ref name="Zalicki">{{cite journal|last1=Zalicki|first1=Piotr|last2=Zare|first2=Richard N.|title=Cavity ring-down spectroscopy for quantitative absorption measurements|journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics|date=February 15, 1995|volume=102|issue=7|pages=2708–2717|doi=10.1063/1.468647|bibcode=1995JChPh.102.2708Z|s2cid=12880938}}</ref> and for [[high performance liquid chromatography]] (HPLC)<ref name="Snyder">{{cite journal|last1=Snyder|first1=KL|last2=Zare|first2=RN|title=Cavity ring-down spectroscopy as a detector for liquid chromatography.|journal=Analytical Chemistry|date=July 1, 2003|volume=75|issue=13|pages=3086–91|pmid=12964755|doi=10.1021/ac0340152|s2cid=13068370}}</ref>  
Zare is also involved in the development of [[desorption electrospray ionization]] (DESI) techniques, which are being used for mass spectrometric imaging of lipids, metabolites and proteins in tissue samples, including prostate cancer.<ref name="Comi">{{cite journal|last1=Comi|first1=Troy J.|last2=Ryu|first2=Seung Woo|last3=Perry|first3=Richard H.|title=Synchronized Desorption Electrospray Ionization Mass Spectrometry Imaging|journal=Analytical Chemistry|date=January 19, 2016|volume=88|issue=2|pages=1169–1175|doi=10.1021/acs.analchem.5b03010|pmid=26569449}}</ref><ref name="Hsu">{{cite journal|last1=Hsu|first1=Cheng-Chih|last2=Chou|first2=Pi-Tai|last3=Zare|first3=Richard N.|title=Imaging of Proteins in Tissue Samples Using Nanospray Desorption Electrospray Ionization Mass Spectrometry|journal=Analytical Chemistry|date=November 17, 2015|volume=87|issue=22|pages=11171–11175|doi=10.1021/acs.analchem.5b03389|pmid=26509582|s2cid=206502281}}</ref><ref name="Banerjee">{{cite journal|last1=Banerjee|first1=Shibdas|last2=Zare|first2=Richard N.|last3=Tibshirani|first3=Robert J.|last4=Kunder|first4=Christian A.|last5=Nolley|first5=Rosalie|last6=Fan|first6=Richard|last7=Brooks|first7=James D.|last8=Sonn|first8=Geoffrey A.|title=Diagnosis of prostate cancer by desorption electrospray ionization mass spectrometric imaging of small metabolites and lipids|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=March 28, 2017|volume=114|issue=13|pages=3334–3339|doi=10.1073/pnas.1700677114|pmid=28292895|pmc=5380053|bibcode=2017PNAS..114.3334B |doi-access=free}}</ref>

{{quote|"I'm right now very excited about mass spectrometry, still excited about lasers, all types of [analytical techniques], but to me, they're tools. They're not ends in themselves... With new tools and measurement techniques, you can make advances in all types of fundamental problems."  Richard Zare<ref name="Mukhopadhyay"/>}}

Zare has also worked with NASA and others on [[astrobiology]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Richard Zare|url=https://nai.nasa.gov/directory/zare-richard/|website=NASA Astrobiology Institute|access-date=March 29, 2017|archive-date=March 30, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170330174454/https://nai.nasa.gov/directory/zare-richard/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Lane">{{cite web|last1=Lane|first1=Neal F.|title=Introducing Dr. Richard Zare's Lecture: Life On Mars|url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/speeches/lane/nl8896.htm|website=National Science Foundation (US)|date=August 8, 1996}}</ref> He is one of the co-authors of a paper that appeared in ''Science'' in 1996, raising the possibility that a meteorite from Mars, [[ALH84001]], contained traces of Martian life.<ref name="McKay"/> Zare used  two-step laser mass spectrometry (L2MS), a technique that is particularly sensitive to organic molecules, to examine samples from the interior of the meteorite.<ref name="Bubbling"/> He found that the  4.5-billion-year-old Martian meteorite, discovered in Antarctica, contained [[polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons]]. This lead researchers to speculate on the presence of fossilized remains from Mars.<ref name="McKay">{{cite journal | last1 = McKay | first1 = D. S. | last2 = Gibson | first2 = E. K. | last3 = Thomas-Keprta | first3 = K. L. | last4 = Vali | first4 = H. | last5 = Romanek | first5 = C. S. | last6 = Clemett | first6 = S. J. | last7 = Chillier | first7 = X. D. F. | last8 = Maechling | first8 = C. R. | last9 = Zare | first9 = R. N. | display-authors = etal | date = 1996 | title = Search for past life on Mars: Possible relic biogenic activity in Martian meteorite ALH84001 | journal = Science | volume = 273 | issue = 5277| pages = 924–930 | doi = 10.1126/science.273.5277.924 | pmid=8688069 | bibcode=1996Sci...273..924M | s2cid = 40690489 }}</ref> Other researchers questioned this interpretation, suggesting that the sample might have been contaminated after its arrival on Earth. Considerable controversy resulted,<ref name="Markley">{{cite book|last1=Markley|first1=Robert|title=Dying planet : Mars in science and the imagination|date=2005|publisher=Duke University Press|location=Durham|isbn=978-0-8223-3638-9|pages=325–326|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=loalUL6vakoC&pg=PA326}}</ref><ref name="Foust">{{cite web|last1=Foust|first1=Jeff|title=Review: The Rock from Mars|date=November 20, 2006|website=The Space Review|url=http://www.thespacereview.com/article/746/1}}</ref> which Zare felt disrupted his ongoing laboratory research.<ref name="Sawyer">{{cite book|last1=Sawyer|first1=Kathy|title=The rock from Mars : a detective story on two planets|date=2006|publisher=Random House|location=New York|isbn=978-1-4000-6010-8|edition=1st|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nQzR6MBmG7AC&q=zare+disrupted&pg=PT368}}</ref> Zare has also worked with NASA on examinations of organic materials obtained from Comet [[81P/Wild]] by the [[Stardust (spacecraft)|Stardust Spacecraft]].<ref name="Sandford">{{cite journal|last1=Sandford|first1=S. ==Publications==
Zare has published several books, including a widely used textbook on the topic of angular momentum in quantum systems that is considered a classic for its explanations of angular momentum algebra and the fundamentals of molecular spectroscopy.<ref name="Bubbling"/>  He is an author or co-author of more than 1,000 peer-reviewed papers.<ref name="Publications">{{cite web|title=Peer-reviewed Publications|url=https://web.stanford.edu/group/Zarelab/pubs.html|website=Zarelab|access-date=July 22, 2019}}</ref>
